links.passage: Drip fertigation is a water and fertilizer management technology that integrates liquids and fertilizers (Zou et al., 2020), which has developed rapidly since its emergence in the 20th century, with significant advantages in precise water supply, fertigation and efficient utilization of water and fertilizer (Bao et al., 2023).
Previous studies had also shown that drip fertigation provide significant advantages in reducing N losses and improving crop yield compared with other irrigation technologies (Li et al., 2020b).

Zheng et al. (2023) reported that while drip fertigation slightly increased 14% NO emissions, it significantly decreased NH3 volatilization (14%), N2O emissions (28%), and NO3
                     - leaching (71%), and significantly increased crop yield (10%), as compared to traditional fertigation practices.

Ding et al. (2023) showed that drip irrigation combined with reduced N application (40% of conventional N application) significantly improved PFPN, WPI and yield, and significantly reduced N2O emissions, in comparison with traditional N application and flood irrigation.

Ding et al. (2023) showed that drip irrigation combined with reduced N application (40% of conventional N application) significantly improved PFPN, WPI and yield, and significantly reduced N2O emissions, in comparison with traditional N application and flood irrigation.

Previous studies have found that reduce fertilization amount under drip irrigation can maintain synchronization between water and N input and demand (Fentabil et al., 2016), thereby improving crop water and N absorption efficiency, reducing N losses, and maintaining yield stably.

Ding et al. (2023) pointed out a 40% reduction in N fertilization under drip irrigation could reduce soil N2O emissions by 45%, improve WPI by 40%, and PFPN by 25%, while maintaining the stability of celery yield.

Zhang et al.(2019) indicated that using 70% conventional N fertilizer application amount under drip irrigation could reduce N2O emissions by 27% and NO emissions by 36%, improve PFPN by 44%, and ensure high crop yield.

Kong et al.(2012) indicated that compared with surface drip irrigation, subsurface drip irrigation combined with different N application rates increased water use efficiency by 17%, sweet pepper yield by 10%, and significantly reducing NO3
                        - leaching.

Kong et al.(2012) indicated that compared with surface drip irrigation, subsurface drip irrigation combined with different N application rates increased water use efficiency by 17%, sweet pepper yield by 10%, and significantly reducing NO3
                        - leaching.

Fertigation can meet the nutrient and water needs of plants, reduce the use of water and fertilizers, provide precise water and nutrient supply for crops, and achieve efficient, economic, green, and sustainable agricultural production (Feng et al., 2023).
